claim: The core library is the product; the CLI is an add-on.
why: The product is the protocol, its vectors and one implementation. Other languages meet it at the JSON format, the CLI or a socket. Lean on existing standards wherever one fits.

claim: Rust, in a new strange-loops repo.
why: A core crate with two allowlisted dependencies, a CLI crate, and the Lean model, vectors and scenarios beside them; the layout enforces the budgets. Reversed from Go in version 31, once phones and browser extensions needed the core itself. The repo keeps its own decisions in .loops/; migration is a collector that lives in the old repo. Version 35 removed step 1's Go core (PR 6): until the data model is formalized, the repo holds the Lean model, its vectors and the JS writer, which stays as an independent second writer for layer 0.

claim: One word per concept, one concept per word.
why: Listed in the Glossary. Record replaces fact; anchor, thing, place and realm absorb genesis, subject, residence and topology; seal retires, so observers emit, vertices tick and a tick covers records; the normative prose is the protocol; LatestBy replaces Upsert. Vertex stays on purpose: it is where loops meet.

claim: A store is a set, not a sequence.
why: Receipt order leaves the fold. Underneath: immutable single-writer segments, content-addressed blobs, a derived index.

claim: Every record has an observer, and two times.
why: Ingestion is a dumb observer reporting what a source holds: hearsay. emitted is the writer's word (RFC 3339); occurred is an optional claimed span that can be coarse.

claim: occurred is a span with a closed grammar: dates, instants and intervals, never a duration.
why: The core reads occurred only to order records and to place them in windows, so each value must name one span, and every store must read it the same way. Calendar dates are UTC days. EDTF Level 1's qualifiers (2009~) and trailing unspecified digits (201X) stay, since each still names one span; a qualifier never changes it. An interval runs between two of those, and its end may be open (2019/..). Spans order by start, then end, an open end last. Durations are refused because an end instant says the same; seasons, open or unknown starts, unknown ends and years past 9999 are refused with occurred-not-span. Accepting more later is free; accepting less would invalidate stored records. Version 35.

claim: Identity is a content hash; signatures sit beside it.
why: A salted payload commitment, an id over the canonical {commit, env}, an Ed25519 signature over loops/record/v1: plus the id. References stay opaque. Records are signed by default and a store carries its writers' key bindings, so it verifies itself. The version in the signed prefix lets a reader refuse only what is newer than it knows.

claim: Writing the same record twice is a no-op.
why: A record's id covers its envelope, including emitted, plus its salt and payload. The same draft written twice is the same record, and set union absorbs it, in a batch or across batches. A new observation gets a fresh salt, so it gets a new id and is simply a new record. Version 35.

claim: A record erases through its envelope field erases; any kind may erase.
why: erases is a set of record ids, refused unless each is one, and never a label. It sits on the envelope, so every reader applies it, whatever its grant. Targets in about were rejected: about: [r:X] already names the thing X anchors, which holds X's revisions too, and a kind would decide which reading applied. No kind is reserved for erasing, so the field carries the meaning by itself, and a revision can erase what it replaces: prev: [r:X], erases: [r:X]. Authority keys on the field. Version 35.

claim: A field belongs on the envelope only if the core reads it.
why: kind, observer, emitted, occurred, about (a set of things), prev (a set), under. derived-from, seen and refs are payload. Unknown envelope fields are refused.

claim: A payload is here, withheld or erased; supersession reads only the envelope.
why: prev sits on the envelope, so withholding or erasing a payload never brings back a record it replaced: no false resurrection. A where test on a missing payload answers unknown, and every result says how many of the records it covers it couldn't read. Added in version 32.

claim: Erasure is per store and small; privacy is withholding, not hiding.
why: An erase removes a payload and keeps its commitment, so ids and ticks still hold. When places hold different forms of a record, the reader keeps the payload if any place has it, erased once an erase record naming it is held, withheld otherwise: a bare erased copy never blanks a payload, and erasure sticks. Disclosure splits by kind when recording. Anything derived is as private as its least-public input and travels under the same grant.

claim: Numbers are what RFC 8785 reads: doubles, exact only within ±(2<sup>53</sup>−1).
why: Past that range two numbers share one canonical form, so writers would disagree on an id. A payload number outside it is refused (number-out-of-range), not kept exactly. The range applies to the number as JCS reads it, so 9007199254740991.1 is accepted as …991. Non-integers are allowed. A number that must stay exact past the range belongs in a string. Version 35.

claim: One checked write path, and what it returns carries the proof.
why: write refuses, in order: a bad envelope, a salt that isn't 16 bytes, a repeated member name at any depth, and an out-of-range number. A batch writes every record through it, and its refusal never depends on the order of drafts or of a prev set. It returns a Written record that carries the proof, so a law that needs distinct member names takes them from the record. Version 35 (PR 7).

claim: Observers are things, with lineages under their names.
why: A lineage id is the hash of its anchor. Names, keys and models are records about a lineage. Names never take part in matching: they resolve at read, through name tables and @home.

claim: Naming, key binding and authority stay separate.
why: Authority is a grant record, pointed to by under. One stance shape covers affirm, adopt, dispute, retire and authorize. A delegate is a shared seat; an identity that emerges starts its own lineage and adopts what it wants to own.

claim: A label may stand in under.
why: A changeset can create a grant @g and act under it in the same batch. under takes labels as about and prev do, counts in cycle detection, and must name a record held in the batch or the store, like prev. It grants nothing extra: whether the grant holds is still decided at read time from its signer's standing, exactly as if it had been written first. Version 35.

claim: Keys in tiers, and presence for what takes effect.
why: A lineage pins its root key; each device has a presence key for standing changes and a device key for emits; agents run on session keys. A record that takes effect because of who signed it needs a person present, and a grant is presence given ahead of time: agents propose and narrow, never widen. Standing ends by retiring through what was held, never by time.

claim: Identity lives in the record, in about.
why: A thing is anchored by the record that starts it, or named by a typed natural key that tooling computes (URLs, birth keys for code); the core only compares strings. Primitives start with the reserved *-anchor kinds. Equivalence (same-as, dispute), provenance and succession stay separate, and resolve-by joins identities at read. An unknown name follows the store's maturity.

claim: A facet is one kind about one thing, emitted whole.
why: Current state is LatestBy per thing, with the kind chosen by from. prev is a set, so a fork shows as several heads, and later links are new records, never edits to about. A record about several things is current in each; a record about nothing anchors a thing of its own, named by its id, and a revision of it is about that id, so unrelated records about nothing never fork each other (version 35).

claim: prev is succession within a thing.
why: A record replaces another only in the things both are about, so a stray prev can't empty another thing's state or break its provenance. You can only replace what you hold: emit refuses a prev naming a record it can't see (prev-unknown) or one about other things (prev-unrelated), and readers refuse a record with a cross-thing prev. Moving or narrowing a record takes an explicit retire about the thing it leaves. Who may replace whom is a rule on envelopes; step 3 supplies it from standing (testimony by its author, facets by standing). Version 34.

claim: A vertex is a question; a store is a thing you write into.
why: A vertex owns neither storage nor sources, and is named by its spec: its id is the hash of the canonical spec and its parameters, and a name record points at the current one. It has no anchor, key or standing, and the same spec with the same parameters is the same vertex wherever it runs (version 32). A store is a lineage with declarations as records and places kept per machine. Schema grows by accretion: dated declarations, no migrations, maturity from open to strict, enforced at admission.

claim: Specs are JSON, stored as records.
why: Defined by JSON Schemas in protocol/ and stored as records of kind vertex; comments are a note; a vertex with params is a template. The core takes specs as data, hashed in canonical form. A spec reads at least one source: one with no from is refused (from-missing), never run empty.

claim: Six folds in two families, plus modifiers.
why: Count, Sum, Min, Max, LatestBy and Collect, with by, where, follow, order, limit, a set mode, and weight-by on Collect's ranking only. Latest is LatestBy with no key, TopN is Collect with an order and a limit, Window is a time bucket used as by, and Avg is Sum and Count divided by the lens. Folds that only accumulate are commutative; folds that follow prev keep the heads and work their answer out from them. Either way the set decides, so a late record folds onto cached state: content order says which record wins, never the order records are read. Numeric folds are exact, the spec hash pins the vocabulary version, and vectors bind implementations. Version 32.

claim: Predicates are a closed, typed set.
why: Six where operators over one record, or the vertex's own state for a boundary. No regex, arithmetic, user code or effects: classify by recording instead. Parse pipelines move into collectors, boundaries lose run, and there is no query language.

claim: where can test any envelope field, named explicitly.
why: Envelope fields are tested as env.kind, env.observer, env.emitted, env.occurred, env.about, env.prev and env.under, and a bare name always means a payload field, so no payload name is shadowed. Envelope tests always answer and choose among heads after supersession. at-least and below on times wait for the time ordering, and observer compares lineage ids until name tables arrive. Version 35.

claim: unread counts only what could change the answer.
why: A record the reader can't read counts as unread only if its payload could change the result. With a limit, that is one newer than the last record kept, or any of them if fewer than the limit were kept; without a limit, every one counts. So unread: 0 means the result is exactly what a reader holding everything would get, whatever the hidden payloads hold: a law to prove, not just a count. Version 35.

claim: Supersession runs over everything held; selection comes after.
why: Each thing's state is worked out over every record the reader holds about it, before any vertex asks. from, envelope tests and payload tests then choose among the heads. Selecting first would bring back a task finished by a record of another kind, revised in a store the vertex doesn't read, closed by a successor a filter drops, or one whose successor is withheld. Counts and sums still include superseded records: they count history. Found while modelling the spec (versions 33 and 34).

claim: A tick is a value; a stored tick is a signed record.
why: A content tick's id is the hash of its vertex, the ids it covers and its result, so two machines compute the same id and anyone holding the records checks it by recomputing. It's written down only when someone cites or sends it, as an ordinary record of kind tick signed by whoever wrote it, so layer 0 keeps one envelope. A witness tick is the same record, covering what the runner had. Once an input is erased, a numeric result rests on that signature instead of recomputation. A tick covers ids, so late ticks never cascade; revisits are new ticks citing old ones. Version 32.

claim: Every result has two names.
why: An input key over everything that shapes it, and a result hash; downstream keys use result hashes, so work stops where results stop changing. Name it, don't carry it. Late records fold onto cached state, so there is no partial rewind to build.

claim: State references form a DAG; ticks may loop.
why: The stale review counters self-reinforcing salience. Hygiene vertices, one per surface, ship as a store's standard vertices.

claim: A place is a location, a format and a scope.
why: Roles are write, hold and blobs: JSONL where git needs it, SQLite where volume does. The index is derived and disposable.

claim: Replication is set union by segment lists.
why: A segment closes once committed, so branches only add files, and a committed segment changing outside an erase is the alarm. A static place is closed segments named by hash plus one mutable segments.json.

claim: A realm is the stores its root name table reaches.
why: Membership is a link, not containment. Across realms: compose by default, bridge only as an explicit signed tick, never replicate. A public store is a standing bridge, declared with presence.

claim: Federation is each person's own store, plus composition.
why: Replies carry the thread's root in about; a ping says only where to look. Admission filters and weight ranks.

claim: A lens is a collector with a base.
why: The base is (tick, lens hash, audience): render, parse the edited file, diff by ids in the core, apply as one changeset. Absence is never an edit. A committed render is a promotion. One tick, many renders; anything a model writes is an observer's record.

claim: Context travels by tick.
why: A reference reaches a reader in one of five states: here, fetchable, withheld, erased, unreachable. Bundles carry only what the receiver can't fetch, filtered by its grant. A session's witness tick is what it knew and retires its key. A brief is a signed record plus a tick by reference. A cloud run is a borrowed place, synced at every tick.

group: The local API and its surfaces
claim: One API under every surface.
why: Pure functions plus a realm handle that narrows to a grant and never widens; identity-aware reads go through fold; tick and witness match the two kinds of tick; refusals are values with closed codes. serve speaks JSON-RPC that mirrors the crate, so the LSP, MCP and front ends are thin translators.

group: The local API and its surfaces
claim: No subscriptions, no coordinator.
why: A watcher holds its own checkpoint. A boundary runs wherever the handle is when the record lands: content ticks anywhere, since a second run makes the same id; witness ticks where their key lives.

group: The local API and its surfaces
claim: The CLI is verb first, with the API's verbs.
why: HTTPie's payload syntax, --json equal to what serve returns, no zoom flags. A batch is one changeset, and labels let records in it refer to each other.

claim: The limits, in four tiers.
why: Not the model, not in the core, not yet (each with a trigger), outside by design. Something enters the core only if two separate cases need it and it can't be built from records, ticks and lenses. No state-machine framework: each vertex already is one.

claim: Budgets guard failures, not size.
why: Tokens per module, the public API diffed, a closed vocabulary priced by the key, a dependency allowlist and inward layering. A budget grows only through a ledger entry that cites the rule for the core. The Go budget checker went with the Go core; budgets return with the Rust core's xtask.

claim: Laws, then vectors, then Rust; no unit tests.
why: A Lean 4 model proves the laws, writes the vectors and is fuzzed against the core, one step ahead of it. Proofs, vectors, differential fuzzing and scenarios all test from outside; expected answers never come from the implementation, and every failure becomes a vector or a scenario.

claim: A law counts only where its boundary establishes its hypotheses.
why: The fold laws held. What failed were the boundaries: a law assumed distinct ids or distinct member names, and nothing guaranteed them. Parsing, writing and settling return types that carry their invariants, as Written does, and the laws take those types. Version 35.

claim: An outside review at each modelling step.
why: A reviewer from another lab gets the code and the docs, never our conclusions. Each finding becomes a vector, a theorem or a narrower claim. Codex found three of our five findings on its own and eight more besides.

claim: Steps 0 and 1 are built; step 2 is modelled and reviewed.
why: The set decides for LatestBy, Count counts repeats, and the keyed-section lens laws hold. Layer 0 agrees byte for byte across the model and an independent JS writer; erasure, sets and member order are proved for any hash. Step 2's model (PR 4) proves the two fold families, per-thing supersession over everything held, settling places and erase records, no false resurrection under any view, honest results, the spec as data and one meaning for a labelled batch. Our review, Codex's and Gemini's found the holes at the boundaries, not in the laws: PR 7 closes the write path, PR 9 gives the envelope erases, and PR 11 gives occurred a closed grammar and an order; 118 vectors in all. Next: formalize the data model in Lean, one record from JSON text to what a reader holds, before step 3 or any Rust.

claim: The design page is built from the repo.
why: Its sections are HTML and its ledger is these records, in design/rethink/. node design/build.mjs renders the page, CI checks the render, projects.gruel.world serves it unlisted, and the claude.ai artifact is a mirror. Once .loops/ exists, the ledger is read from it. Version 35.
